title: What is the difference between AWS Systems Manager (SSM — broad fleet management: Run Command, Session Manager, Parameter Store, inventory, automation) and Patch Manager (a feature within SSM for OS/application patching with baselines and maintenance windows)?
shortTitle: AWS Systems Manager (SSM) versus Patch Manager — broad fleet management versus OS/application patching

s1_definition.profdef: AWS Systems Manager (SSM) is a broad operations-management service that gives you a single control plane over a fleet of EC2 instances, on-premises servers, and other managed nodes. It bundles many capabilities: Run Command for executing scripts remotely, Session Manager for shell access without SSH keys or open ports, Parameter Store for configuration and secrets, State Manager for desired-state enforcement, Inventory for collecting software metadata, and Automation for runbooks. Patch Manager is one feature inside Systems Manager, specialized for a single job: applying operating-system and application patches to those managed nodes using patch baselines (rules about which patches are approved) and maintenance windows (approved time slots when patching may run).
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine Systems Manager is the entire facilities-and-operations department for every branch building the bank owns. That department can unlock any door remotely (Session Manager), send a work order to every branch at once (Run Command), keep a master list of every piece of equipment in every branch (Inventory), store the shared keys and policies in a locked cabinet (Parameter Store), and run multi-step repair procedures (Automation). Patch Manager is one specialist team inside that department whose only job is to keep the building's locks, alarms, and safety systems up to date. That team follows an approved list of which upgrades are allowed (the patch baseline) and is only allowed to do noisy maintenance work during fixed off-hours windows so customers are not disturbed (the maintenance window).
s1_definition.oneliner: Systems Manager is the whole operations toolbox for your fleet; Patch Manager is the one tool in that box that keeps the fleet patched on approved rules during approved windows.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** AWS Systems Manager (SSM) is a broad operations-management service that gives you a single control plane over a fleet of EC2 instances, on-premises servers, and other managed nodes. It bundles many capabilities: Run Command for executing scripts remotely, Session Manager for shell access without SSH keys or open ports, Parameter Store for configuration and secrets, State Manager for desired-state enforcement, Inventory for collecting software metadata, and Automation for runbooks. Patch Manager is one feature inside Systems Manager, specialized for a single job: applying operating-system and application patches to those managed nodes using patch baselines (rules about which patches are approved) and maintenance windows (approved time slots when patching may run).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine Systems Manager is the entire facilities-and-operations department for every branch building the bank owns. That department can unlock any door remotely (Session Manager), send a work order to every branch at once (Run Command), keep a master list of every piece of equipment in every branch (Inventory), store the shared keys and policies in a locked cabinet (Parameter Store), and run multi-step repair procedures (Automation). Patch Manager is one specialist team inside that department whose only job is to keep the building's locks, alarms, and safety systems up to date. That team follows an approved list of which upgrades are allowed (the patch baseline) and is only allowed to do noisy maintenance work during fixed off-hours windows so customers are not disturbed (the maintenance window).

**One line to remember:** Systems Manager is the whole operations toolbox for your fleet; Patch Manager is the one tool in that box that keeps the fleet patched on approved rules during approved windows.

sections.s2_technical:
Systems Manager works through the SSM Agent, a small program that runs on each managed node and polls the Systems Manager service for instructions. Because the agent polls outbound over HTTPS, you do not need to open any inbound ports — this is why Session Manager can give you a shell on an instance in a private subnet with no bastion host, no SSH key, and no inbound security-group rule. The node must have an IAM instance profile that allows it to talk to Systems Manager, typically the managed policy `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`.

Run Command lets you execute a documented command (an SSM Document) across many nodes at once. For example, you can run a shell script on every node tagged `Environment=prod` in one API call, with output captured to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs. In Java you would trigger this with the AWS SDK: `ssmClient.sendCommand(SendCommandRequest.builder().documentName("AWS-RunShellScript").targets(Target.builder().key("tag:Environment").values("prod").build()).parameters(Map.of("commands", List.of("systemctl restart bank-api"))).build())` which returns a `SendCommandResponse` carrying a command ID you poll for status.

Parameter Store holds configuration values and secrets in a hierarchy, with optional KMS encryption for `SecureString` parameters. A Spring Boot banking service reads its database password without hardcoding it: `ssmClient.getParameter(GetParameterRequest.builder().name("/bank/prod/db-password").withDecryption(true).build()).parameter().value()`.

Inventory collects metadata — installed applications, OS versions, network config — from each node on a schedule so you can answer "which servers still run an outdated TLS library?" across the whole fleet. State Manager enforces a desired state, re-applying a configuration document on a schedule so drift is corrected automatically. Automation runs multi-step runbooks, for example "snapshot the volume, stop the instance, resize it, start it, verify health."

Patch Manager sits inside all of this and reuses the same agent and maintenance-window machinery, but its job is narrow. A patch baseline is a rule set: which classification of patches (security, critical), which severity, and an auto-approval delay (for example, approve security patches seven days after release so you are not the first to hit a bad patch). A patch group is a tag that associates specific instances with a specific baseline — production can use a conservative baseline with a long approval delay while a test patch group uses an aggressive one. A maintenance window is the scheduled, time-boxed slot during which patching tasks are allowed to run, so you never patch a trade-settlement server in the middle of the trading day. The senior-level nuance is that Patch Manager is not a separate product you buy or a separate agent you install; it is a feature that depends entirely on Systems Manager being set up correctly first — the agent, the instance role, and connectivity to the SSM endpoints must already work before Patch Manager can do anything.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the platform team runs a fleet of EC2 instances across two environments. Rajesh is a software engineer whose savings-account service runs on production instances, and Priya owns the property-loan service running on a separate set. The operations team faces several real problems.

Problem 1 — The security team reports a critical operating-system vulnerability and asks, "which of our servers are affected, and when will they all be patched?" Right now nobody can answer quickly because patching is done by hand, server by server, over SSH. This is exactly what Patch Manager solves: you define a baseline that approves security patches, group the servers, and schedule the patching into an off-hours maintenance window so it happens consistently and is reported centrally.

Problem 2 — An engineer needs to restart the banking API on twenty production servers at once after a config change. Logging into each one with SSH is slow and error-prone, and the auditors dislike that SSH keys are floating around. This is exactly what Run Command and Session Manager solve: one API call targets all servers by tag, with no SSH keys and a full audit trail of who ran what.

Problem 3 — The database password is currently sitting in a properties file, which the compliance team flagged. This is exactly what Parameter Store solves: the password lives encrypted in Parameter Store and the application fetches it at startup.

The code models this control plane in plain Java so the distinction is crystal clear. We build a `FleetOperationsManager` that represents Systems Manager and exposes broad operations — `runCommand`, `openSession`, `getParameter`, `collectInventory`. Inside it we build a `PatchManager` that represents the narrow patching feature and depends on the same fleet. We define `ManagedNode` (a server), `PatchBaseline` (approval rules), `MaintenanceWindow` (allowed time slot), and a demo that shows SSM doing broad work and Patch Manager doing its one specialized job within an approved window.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -jar target/fleet-ops-service-1.0.0.jar

# In real AWS, the equivalent CLI calls are:
# Broad SSM — run a command across prod nodes:
aws ssm send-command \
  --document-name "AWS-RunShellScript" \
  --targets "Key=tag:Environment,Values=prod" \
  --parameters 'commands=["systemctl restart bank-api"]'

# Narrow Patch Manager — register a baseline and run patching in a window:
aws ssm create-patch-baseline --name "bank-prod-baseline" \
  --approval-rules "PatchRules=[{PatchFilterGroup={...},ApproveAfterDays=7}]"
aws ssm start-session --target i-savings01   # Session Manager, no SSH key
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a fleet of four managed nodes (three production, one test), a patch baseline approving Security and Critical patches with a seven-day delay, and a maintenance window of 2 AM to 5 AM.

Step 1: The application builds the fleet. Each `ManagedNode` carries its tags, including `PatchGroup`. At this point no node is patched. The data lives in the `FleetOperationsManager`'s list.

Step 2: Systems Manager performs broad operations. `putParameter` stores the encrypted database password in Parameter Store; `getParameter` proves the application can read it at startup instead of from a properties file. The secret value never appears in code.

Step 3: `runCommand` targets every node tagged `Environment=prod` and issues a restart. Three nodes match; the command fans out to all three in one call. No SSH key is used.

Step 4: `openSession` on `i-savings01` represents Session Manager giving a shell with no inbound port open. `inventoryByOs` answers the auditor's question — four nodes run Amazon Linux 2.

Step 5: Patch Manager is asked to patch the `prod` group with a Security patch at 11:30 AM. The baseline approves Security, but the maintenance window is closed at 11:30, so Patch Manager refuses and logs a warning. Nothing changes.

Step 6: Patch Manager is asked again at 2:30 AM. Now the classification is approved and the window is open, so the three production nodes are marked patched. The test node is untouched because it is in a different patch group.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-25 02:30:00 INFO    Fetched secret from Parameter Store: true
2026-10-25 02:30:00 INFO    Run Command on 3 nodes [systemctl restart bank-api]
2026-10-25 02:30:00 INFO    Session Manager shell opened on i-savings01 (no SSH, no bastion)
2026-10-25 02:30:00 INFO    Inventory: nodes on Amazon Linux 2 = 4
2026-10-25 02:30:00 WARNING Maintenance window CLOSED at 11:30 — refusing to patch production
2026-10-25 02:30:00 INFO    Patched 3 nodes in group prod (Security, delay 7d)
2026-10-25 02:30:00 INFO    Production nodes patched this run: 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
AWS Systems Manager is the broad operations-management service that gives you one control plane over an entire fleet of servers, whether those servers are EC2 instances or on-premises machines. It bundles many capabilities: Run Command for executing scripts across many nodes at once, Session Manager for getting a shell without SSH keys or open inbound ports, Parameter Store for configuration and encrypted secrets, Inventory for collecting software metadata, State Manager for enforcing desired state, and Automation for multi-step runbooks. Patch Manager is not a separate product — it is one feature inside Systems Manager whose single job is applying operating-system and application patches using patch baselines and maintenance windows.

The relationship is the key point. Patch Manager depends entirely on Systems Manager being set up first: the SSM Agent must run on each node, the node must have the instance role that allows it to talk to Systems Manager, and connectivity to the SSM endpoints must exist. Once that foundation is there, Patch Manager reuses the same agent and the same maintenance-window machinery. A patch baseline is a rule set that says which patch classifications are approved and how many days to wait after release before approving, so you are never the first to apply a potentially bad patch. A patch group is just a tag that maps specific servers to a specific baseline, so production can run a conservative baseline while a test group runs an aggressive one. A maintenance window is the time-boxed slot during which disruptive patching is allowed to run.

The way I explain the difference in one sentence is that Systems Manager is the whole operations toolbox and Patch Manager is the one specialized tool in that box for keeping the fleet patched. If someone asks me to restart a banking service across twenty servers, store a database password securely, or answer an auditor's question about which servers run an outdated library, that is all Systems Manager. If someone asks me to make sure every production server gets this month's critical security patches, but only during the approved off-hours window and only patches that have passed the approval delay, that is specifically Patch Manager.

At the National Bank of India I used this split directly. We moved the database password out of a properties file into Parameter Store as a KMS-encrypted SecureString, which the Spring Boot service reads at startup, and that closed a compliance finding. We used Session Manager so engineers get audited shell access to instances in private subnets with no bastion host and no SSH keys floating around. And we used Patch Manager with a conservative production baseline — security and critical patches only, a seven-day approval delay — scheduled into a 2 AM Sunday maintenance window, so our trade-settlement and savings-account servers are never patched during the trading day. The broad toolbox handled day-to-day operations, and the narrow patching feature handled compliance-driven patching on strict rules, which is exactly the division of labor the two are designed for.
